evidence_items.source_text: A woman in her 60s presented to her primary care physician for further evaluation of abdominal pain. She had undergone elective surgical repair of idiopathic scoliosis 3 weeks prior. She had a history of breast cancer remotely requiring bilateral mastectomy, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, hypertension and hypothyroidism. There was no family history of gastrointestinal or musculoskeletal malignancy. She had reported to have been recovering well from spinal surgery other than having abdominal discomfort that waxed and waned in intensity, which was apparent postoperatively. She did not require analgesic medications for her spine but was requiring analgesic relief for the ongoing abdominal discomfort. Her abdominal wall pain was deemed related to a small haematoma based on initial CT radiological findings. She was informed it would ultimately resolve over time. Her abdominal pain had escalated seeking her to see care at a local emergency department three times prior to presentation to her primary care physician. She denied fever, chills or sweats. Her main symptom was midline abdominal discomfort. On our initial examination, she had midline abdominal pain with a lump of the midline. Her pain was out of proportion to examination. There was no induration or fluctuance. Her postoperative spinal scar was healing well, and her examination was otherwise unremarkable.
Laboratory investigations yielded normal blood counts, normal chemistry panels and urine studies. There was a mildly abnormal alkaline phosphatase deemed related to recent spinal surgery.

CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast revealed no acute abnormality in the abdomen or pelvis and revealed postoperative changes of the spine without acute abnormalities. She had a hyperdense lesion of the midline abdominal wall measuring 2.2×1.7 cm, which was felt to be a small haematoma (figure 1).

Repeat CT was performed through the emergency department at a return visit as a result of increased pain and failure of outpatient supportive therapy with analgesics within a few weeks of initial imaging. This showed small 3.2×1.5 cm subcutaneous hyperdense lesion in the upper midline abdominal wall, increased in size when compared with the prior CT.
An ultrasound was significant for 2.9×2.1×1.5 cm irregular lobulated hypoechoic mass in the left paramedian abdominal wall with internal vascularity in which biopsy was advised (figure 2).
Soft tissue pathology demonstrated spindle cell proliferation, consistent with DF.
She underwent surgical resection of the mass with abdominal wall repair with mesh. Postoperatively, she reported that her pain had resolved and recovered uneventfully.
Final pathology was consistent with preoperative diagnosis of DF, and margins were negative (figure 3).
